title: Targeted AAV Vector Transduction of Intradental Neurons in Mice
author: Liu, Chang, et al.

steps.title: Attach suture to retractors
steps.instruction: Attach the black braided suture to the lateral retractors.

steps.title: Prepare silk fibroin aliquots
steps.instruction: Prepare silk fibroin at 50 mg/mL in 50 µL aliquots and store them at –80 °C.

steps.title: Prepare AAV aliquots
steps.instruction: Prepare AAV6.2‑iCre at 7.2×10¹² vg/mL in 2.5 µL aliquots and store them at –80 °C.

steps.title: Thaw reagents on ice
steps.instruction: Thaw 2.5 µL aliquots of silk fibroin (50 mg/mL) and AAV6.2‑iCre (7.2×10¹² vg/mL) on ice; keep the thawed silk fibroin at 4 °C (stable for 1 month) and the thawed AAV at 4 °C (stable for 1 week).

steps.title: Mix AAV with silk fibroin
steps.instruction: Combine equal volumes of the viral vector and silk fibroin at a 1:1 ratio, mix gently, spin down, and keep the mixture on ice.

substeps.instruction: Pipette silk fibroin into the viral vector.
Pipette up and down gently to mix.
Spin down the mixture in a mini‑centrifuge at maximum speed (RCF ≈ 2,000 × g).

steps.title: Eject composite bead
steps.instruction: Eject a 0.5–1 mm diameter bead of dental composite onto a working surface.

steps.title: Pick up paper point
steps.instruction: Use forceps to pick up an endodontic paper point.

steps.title: Load composite onto point
steps.instruction: Collect a small amount of flowable composite (approximately the size of a pin head) on the tip of the endodontic paper point.

steps.title: Cover preparation with composite
steps.instruction: Place the composite‑loaded paper point onto the tooth preparation and cover the pulp horns with the composite.

steps.title: Remove excess composite
steps.instruction: Use a clean endodontic paper point to remove any excess composite and prevent over‑loading of the restoration material.

steps.title: Light‑cure composite
steps.instruction: Light‑cure the composite for 10 seconds, keeping the curing light at an adequate distance from the tooth to avoid heating.

steps.title: Remove retractors
steps.instruction: Gently remove the lateral retractors from the mouse.

steps.title: Detach retraction cord
steps.instruction: Detach the retraction cord from the mandibular incisors.

steps.title: Detach composite from incisors
steps.instruction: Detach any remaining composite from the upper incisors.

steps.title: Remove nose cone
steps.instruction: Remove the nose cone from the mouse.

steps.title: Confirm recovery
steps.instruction: Ensure the mouse is awake, recovered in a clean cage, and then return it to its home cage.

steps.title: Verify labeling after 3 weeks
steps.instruction: Three weeks post‑application, perform trigeminal ganglion (TG) screening to visualize the TG surface and verify AAV labeling efficiency; note that expression may be detectable earlier but should be empirically determined.

description: The first successful labeling of neurons innervating the inner tooth (i.e., intradental neurons) was reported in 1956, utilizing silver impregnation.2 Over subsequent decades, a variety of chemical tracers have been developed and employed for neuron labeling in dental and sensory research. These include horseradish peroxidase (HRP),3,4 HRP conjugated with wheat germ agglutinin (HRP-WGA),5 Fluorogold,6 Dil and DiO,7 non-fluorophore-conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (non-fluor. CTB),8,9 and more recently, fluorophore-conjugated CTB (fluor. CTB).10,11,12 In parallel, adeno-associated virus (AAV) systems have gained prominence as powerful, flexible tools for transducing neurons, offering high efficiency, long-term labeling, and reduced toxicity for long-term studies. Notably, cell-type-specific capsid selection strategies such as the Cre recombinase-based AAV targeted evolution (CREATE) platform, introduced by Dr. Deverman et al.,13 and further optimized by Dr. Chan et al.,14 have revolutionized the specificity and efficiency of neuronal targeting through modified capsid proteins. Specifically, AAV6.2 – also referred to as AAV6(F129L) – has been shown to transduce airway epithelium, muscle and lung tissues, as described by Dr. Limberis et al., and Dr. van Lieshout et al.,.15,16 For a detailed comparison of these labeling methods including their discovery dates, molecular types, efficiency, specificity, and tissue applications please refer to Table 1 below.Table 1Comparison of existing methods for labeling efficiency and specificityDiscovery yearMethodLabels cell body or fibersInjection & labeling timeLabeling efficiencyCNS/Sensory labeling (tooth?)SpeciesImaging resolution for fibersSpecificityToxicity1956Silver impregnation2Fibers (mainly); some cell bodiesVariable, slow (hours–days after fixation)ModerateSensory (Tooth: Yes)HumanLM, moderateModerate, not cell-type specificLow (can be harsh fixatives)1981, 1984HRP3,4Cell bodies & fibers (mainly retrograde)Pulp Injecti
